With technology stocks retreating amid concerns about lofty AI valuations and massive infrastructure spending, investors may want to consider defensive healthcare stocks that are showing impressive relative strength. Notably, AbbVie ABBV) and Eli Lilly LLY) stocks have hit fresh 52-week highs after posting strong Q3 results last week, highlighting investors' appetite for established healthcare companies with resilient demand, strong earnings potential, and attractive long-term growth prospects. Both stocks are up more than 25% in 2026 and have outperformed the broader market with returns of more than 100% in the last three years. Hitting a fresh 52-week high of $302 a share on Thursday, AbbVie's ascent has been supported by strong demand for its blockbuster immunology treatments Skyrizi and Rinvoq. AbbVie's Q3 revenue climbed 10% year over year to $17.4 billion, with adjusted earnings more than doubling to $3.82 per share. Management also raised its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to a range of $13.95-$13.99, which would reflect more than 39% growth. Adding to its defensive appeal, AbbVie recently announced a 5.2% dividend increase for 2027 to a quarterly payout of $1.82 per share, reinforcing its commitment to shareholder returns with a dividend yield comfortably above 2%. Eli Lilly has emerged as one of the medical sector's strongest growth stories, with LLY shares also hitting a 52-week peak in today's trading session of $1,453 a share. Demand for blockbuster diabetes and obesity treatments Mounjaro and Zepbound continues to fuel exceptional growth. In Q3, revenue surged 39% YoY to $24.4 billion, prompting management to raise its full-year sales guidance to $91-$92 billion, reflecting 40% growth from $65.18 billion in fiscal 2025. Although Lilly trades at a premium to many of its healthcare peers at 40X forward earnings, its expanding obesity treatment franchise and robust drug pipeline provide compelling long-term growth catalysts that are less directly tied to economic cycles. With technology volatility intensifying, AbbVie and Eli Lilly offer attractive ways to diversify into healthcare while maintaining exposure to long-term growth. ABBV stands out for its dividend income and defensive characteristics, while LLY offers stronger growth potential, albeit with greater valuation risk. Although they warrant some caution near 52-week highs, both stocks could be worthwhile portfolio additions for investors seeking greater stability outside the technology sector.  closed recently with the sort of release that dividend-focused observers hope to see from a large pharmaceutical group: higher revenue, a lifted earnings outlook, and an increased quarterly payout. The Chicago-area drugmaker posted that sales rose at a healthy pace, driven by its several flagship immunology medicines, while its former blockbuster Humira continued its planned slide as biosimilar competition deepened. The company also confirmed that it had completed the acquisition of Apogee, adding late-stage candidates for inflammatory disease. This analysis explains how the quarter was built, why the immunology franchise matters so much to the income thesis, what the neuroscience and aesthetics lines reveal, and where the risks lie. Revenue grew at roughly a notable level clip on both a posted and operational basis, a strong showing for a company of this size and for a business that has had to absorb the loss of exclusivity on its biggest historical product. Adjusted earnings per share came in comfortably, even after absorbing a charge for acquired in-process research and milestone payments, which management always includes in its results because they come with its business development approach. The company then raised its adjusted earnings per share range for the full year, narrowing and lifting the band. That range already embeds the year-to-date research charges, which is a useful reminder that guidance for this company is not a clean operating number but one burdened by deal-related expense. Posted earnings sit well below adjusted earnings, as is typical for a group with heavy intangible amortization after earlier large acquisitions. Immunology remains the heart of the enterprise. Skyrizi and Rinvoq each grew at a strong double-digit pace, and together they now generate far more revenue than Humira did at the point when its decline began to be noticeable. Humira itself fell sharply, the expected consequence of biosimilar erosion in the United States and elsewhere. That arithmetic is the core of the capital spending narrative. Years ago, analysts feared that Humira's patent cliff would leave a gaping hole. Instead, the company engineered a replacement cycle with new molecules, broader labels and aggressive launch execution. The latest quarter shows the replacement not only complete in revenue terms but also still growing. A further regulatory milestone arrived with approval of a subcutaneous induction option for Skyrizi in Crohn's disease, which may simplify treatment initiation for patients and physicians. Neuroscience grew faster than the group average, reflecting sizeable contributions from Vraylar, Botox in therapeutic uses, the migraine pair Ubrelvy and Qulipta, and the Parkinson's disease therapy Vyalev. Each product addresses a chronic condition with durable demand, so the segment adds a layer of stability beneath the more cyclical immunology story. The regulatory calendar also helped. A new Parkinson's option based on tavapadon received approval, expanding the company's presence in movement disorders. Such additions matter because they reduce reliance on any single molecule and give the sales force broader conversations with neurologists. Diversification is a standing theme in pharma dividend analysis. Not every line advanced. Aesthetics edged lower overall, with the toxin franchise growing modestly while the dermal filler brand declined. Consumer-funded procedures respond to confidence and discretionary spending, and competitive launches in filler have added pressure. The company has described aesthetics as a recovery story that depends on consumer sentiment normalising. Oncology was nearly flat. Venclexta and Elahere contributed meaningful sales, but the older Imbruvica franchise continued to erode due to competition and regulatory price effects. These softer areas show why a single strong quarter is not a guarantee. Moves of this kind are often read against the wider S&P 500. For AbbVie

The company increased the quarterly dividend by a notable level, payable early next year. For a company that has lifted its distribution for many consecutive years, the move preserves a track record that income-oriented owners prize. The increase was more modest than some earlier steps, which fits a larger base and the heavy research spending the company carries. Sustainability depends on cash flow, and the company's cash generation has historically been ample relative to payout. The company has also been explicit that business development and the dividend are both priorities. The balance requires discipline: acquisitions funded by debt can raise interest costs, which in turn tighten the room for future dividend growth. The latest release improves the picture on the third item, with immunology momentum offsetting legacy erosion, while leverage will be shaped by how large deals are financed. Companies with long dividend records face a psychological burden: a pause or cut would be treated as a regime change. AbbVie's guidance includes a per-unit charge for acquired in-process research and development, which the company updates quarter by quarter as deals close. This makes the stated range somewhat unusual: it moves not only when operating performance changes but whenever new transactions are booked. A raised range despite a larger charge implies that underlying operating strength more than covered the extra expense. That treatment differs from some peers that exclude such items entirely. Analysts therefore sometimes add the charge back to compare against rivals. Neither approach is wrong, but consistency matters when evaluating quality of earnings across the sector. The practical lesson is to read the footnotes. Several programs received mention in the release. A regulatory submission was made for etentamig in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Temab-A earned breakthrough therapy designations, a status intended to accelerate development of promising oncology candidates. An early compound will advance into a mid-stage study for chronic weight management, signalling entry into a crowded and closely watched obesity field. Pipeline news carries high variance. Many compounds fail in later stages, and designations do not guarantee approval. Even so, the breadth of assets across immunology, oncology and neuroscience illustrates a management strategy of keeping multiple shots on goal rather than relying on one blockbuster. title: What Could AbbVie Stock Be Worth In Three Years? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. AbbVie (ABBV) stock returned 40.6% in the year to November 4, 2026, against 14.9% for the S&P 500. You may hold it after that run or be thinking of buying. Either way, the company’s profit is hard to project because AbbVie’s net income more than quadrupled in the twelve months to September 2026 from a year earlier. So what would a share bought today be worth if AbbVie keeps growing? Based on AbbVie’s own figures, a scenario shows that a share bought at $294.83 on November 4, 2026, would be worth about $328.03 three years later. That represents an 11.3% upside before dividends. In that scenario, sales grow 9.1% a year, a rate that equals 85% of AbbVie’s latest twelve-month pace of 10.7%. The net margin ends at a blend of 70% of today’s level and 30% of its average at the twelve quarter ends before the latest one. The P/E stays at today’s level. This multiple sits below its 69.5 average at ten quarter ends from December 2023 to September 2026, leaving out readings above 100. The share count stays at today’s level. AbbVie’s diluted count rose about 0.06% over the three years to September 2026, and if that pattern went on, each share would get slightly less. Here is how AbbVie today compares with the scenario three years on. Higher sales produce all of the gain, though the scenario’s lower net margin offsets part of it. None of the upside comes from the P/E. Most of AbbVie’s sales growth comes from its immunology drugs, led by Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Immunology revenue approached $9.2 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, up 16.6% on an operational basis. On its October 30, 2026 call, management said it expects to deliver top-tier growth again in 2027. Management also said Skyrizi and Rinvoq are adding about $6 billion of sales combined in 2026, even with more competition. Skyrizi alone sold $17.6 billion in fiscal 2025, an increase of 49.9% from a year earlier. Those gains have to keep outrunning AbbVie’s losses elsewhere. Humira sales fell 30.6% in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, to $683 million. Management put this decline down to continued competition from biosimilar copies. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue outlook to about $67.8 billion. Three of that year’s quarters are already reported, so the outlook is mostly results already in hand, not a pace for later years. How AbbVie’s Upside Changes Under Other Assumptions Each row below changes one assumption while keeping the other two as they are in the scenario. The scenario bases its sales growth on AbbVie’s fastest pace of the past three years. Twelve-month revenue growth was 0.7% in the period to September 2024 and 7.4% a year later. Today’s net margin is also nearly twice its average at the twelve quarter ends from September 2023 to June 2026, so the margin in the scenario is set lower. Taken one at a time, three years of owning AbbVie stock would return nothing, before dividends, if revenue growth slowed to 5.3% a year. That compares with 10.7% in the twelve months to September 2026. Owning the stock would also return nothing if the net margin fell to 12.1% in year three, against 15.7% today. The same holds if the P/E fell to 45.3, against 50.4 at the November 4, 2026 close. AbbVie’s twelve-month net margin is the measure to watch when the company reports its fiscal fourth quarter, expected in February 2027.
